name: Permutations, Combinations & Probability
intro: **Ask "does the order matter?" before writing anything.** That single question decides between a permutation and a combination and settles most of the topic (§1).
For "at least one", always count the complement. For "not together", count the total minus the together-case. Both are §4 and §14.

qs.q: In how many ways can the letters of the word CHAIR be arranged?
qs.h: §2 — five distinct letters, so it is simply 5!.

qs.q: The value of ⁸C₃ is
In how many ways can 3 distinct prizes be given to 5 students if no student may receive more than one?
qs.h: §1 — the prizes are distinct, so order matters: this is ⁵P₃.

qs.q: The number of ways to select a committee of 3 from 10 people is
qs.h: §8 — a committee is unordered, so use ¹⁰C₃.

qs.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1 to 9 if repetition is allowed?
qs.h: §7 — each of the three places has 9 independent choices. There is no zero to worry about here.

qs.q: In how many ways can 6 people be seated in a row if two particular people must sit together?
qs.h: §3 — glue the pair into a single block, arrange 5 objects, then arrange within the block.

qs.q: In how many ways can the letters of ORANGE be arranged so that the vowels are never all together?
qs.h: §4 — total minus the together-case. Never count "not together" directly.

qs.q: In how many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls stand in a row so that no two girls are together?
qs.h: §4 — seat the boys first, then place the girls into the gaps between and around them. Five boys create six gaps.

qs.q: In how many ways can 4 books be arranged on a shelf if one particular book must be first?
qs.h: §3 — fix the constrained object, then arrange whatever remains freely.

qs.q: In how many ways can the letters of LEADING be arranged so that the vowels always come together?
qs.h: §3 — the three vowels form one block, leaving 5 objects to arrange.

qs.q: Find the number of distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA.
qs.h: §5 — divide by the factorial of each repeat count: three A's and two N's.

qs.q: The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI is
qs.h: §5 — four I's, four S's and two P's.

qs.q: In how many ways can 7 people be seated around a circular table?
qs.h: §6 — fix one person to kill the rotational symmetry, giving (n − 1)!.

qs.q: The number of ways to seat 8 people around a round table with two particular people together is
qs.h: §6 + §3 — block the pair, then apply the circular rule to the 7 resulting objects.

qs.q: How many different necklaces can be made from 6 distinct beads?
qs.h: §6 — a necklace can be flipped, so divide the circular count by a further 2.

qs.q: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 0–9 without repetition?
qs.h: §7 — the leading digit cannot be 0, so handle that place first.

qs.q: How many 3-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
qs.h: §7 — fix the unit digit first, since that is where the constraint lives.

qs.q: From 7 men and 5 women, in how many ways can a committee of 5 be formed containing exactly 3 men?
qs.h: §8 — choose each group separately and multiply.

qs.q: In how many ways can a team of 4 be chosen from 6 boys and 4 girls if it must include at least one girl?
qs.h: §14 — "at least one" means total minus the all-boys case.

qs.q: How many 5-digit numbers divisible by 5 can be formed from the digits 0–9 without repetition?
qs.h: §7 — split into two cases by the unit digit, because a unit digit of 5 restricts the leading digit further.
qs.s: Unit 0: 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3024. Unit 5: the leading digit has 8 choices ⟹ 8 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 2688. Total = 5712.

qs.q: A fair die is rolled twice. Find the probability that the sum is 7 (as a fraction).
qs.h: §13 — count the favourable ordered pairs over 36.
qs.s: 6 of the 36 ordered pairs sum to 7 ⟹ 1/6.

qs.q: Two cards are drawn from a standard pack. The probability that both are aces is
qs.h: §13 — ⁴C₂/⁵²C₂, or sequentially (4/52)(3/51). The second card's denominator changes.
qs.s: (4/52)(3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221. (1/169 treats the draws as independent — the planted error.)

qs.q: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn at random. Find the probability that both are red (as a fraction).
qs.h: §13 — ⁵C₂ over ⁸C₂.

qs.q: A coin is tossed 4 times. The probability of getting at least one head is
qs.h: §14 — take the complement: no head at all.

qs.q: The probability that A solves a problem is 1/3 and that B solves it is 1/4. Find the probability that the problem is solved (as a fraction).
qs.h: §14 — the complement of "neither solves it". Adding 1/3 and 1/4 double-counts the overlap.

qs.q: Three fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one shows heads, the probability that all three are heads is
qs.h: §15 — conditioning shrinks the sample space from 8 outcomes to 7.

qs.q: Find the number of distinct arrangements of the letters of SUCCESS.
qs.h: Three S's and two C's.

qs.q: The number of diagonals of a polygon with 12 sides is
qs.h: ¹²C₂ counts all the segments; subtract the 12 sides.

qs.q: In how many ways can 5 distinct letters be posted into 3 letter boxes?
qs.h: Each letter independently picks a box.
qs.s: 3⁵ = 243. (5³ answers a different question — boxes picking letters.)

qs.q: The number of handshakes among 15 people, each shaking hands once with every other, is
qs.h: ¹⁵C₂ — a handshake is unordered.

qs.q: In how many ways can 4 identical balls be placed in 3 distinct boxes?
qs.h: Stars and bars: C(n + r − 1, r − 1) for identical objects.

qs.q: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 100. The probability that it is divisible by 3 or 5 is
qs.h: Inclusion–exclusion: subtract the multiples of 15.

qs.q: In how many ways can a person go from the bottom-left to the top-right corner of a 4 × 3 grid, moving only right or up?
qs.h: Choose which of the 7 moves are the 3 upward ones.

qs.q: The rank of the word RANK among all arrangements of its letters in dictionary order is
qs.h: Count everything alphabetically before it, letter position by letter position.
qs.s: Words starting A, K or N: 3 × 3! = 18. Then RAKN is 19th and RANK is 20th.

qs.q: Five letters are placed at random into five addressed envelopes. In how many ways does no letter reach its correct envelope?
qs.h: §10 — this is the derangement D₅.

qs.q: Two dice are thrown. The probability that the product of the numbers is even is
qs.h: The complement: an odd product needs both dice odd.

audit: using a permutation where the selection is unordered, or vice versa (§1)
counting the restricted case directly instead of taking the complement (§4, §14)
placing the constrained group first — always seat the unconstrained items and use the gaps
not dividing by the factorials of the repeat counts (§5)
using n! for a circular arrangement, or forgetting the extra ÷2 for a necklace (§6)
filling the free places before the constrained one
treating draws without replacement as independent (§13)
using the unconditional probability where the sample space has already shrunk (§15)
raising the wrong quantity to the wrong power in a distribution problem (§9)
using distinct-object logic for identical balls
miscounting the blocks of words that precede the target (§12)
